PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 62 — Lesson 86: Interprofessional Collaboration, Team-Based Care & Care Coordination

FNP-level goal: Coordinate care so the patient experiences one coherent plan rather than disconnected visits. Clarify roles, communicate clinical uncertainty, integrate pharmacy, nursing, behavioral health, rehabilitation, social support, and specialty care, and maintain ownership of results, referrals, medication changes, and escalation.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate multidisciplinary work from truly coordinated interprofessional care.
  • Define the FNP’s role in shared care, consultation, delegation, referral, and closed-loop follow-up.
  • Use structured communication to reduce omission during handoffs and escalation.
  • Identify medication, diagnostic, and access risks at transitions between clinicians and settings.
  • Engage pharmacists, nurses, social workers, behavioral-health clinicians, rehabilitation professionals, and specialists appropriately.
  • Recognize when fragmented care or role ambiguity creates an urgent patient-safety problem.

Part 1 — A Team Is Not Automatically Coordinated Care

Many clinicians may touch one chart without creating a shared plan. Multidisciplinary care means several disciplines contribute; interprofessional care requires communication, role clarity, mutual respect, and coordinated action around patient goals. The patient and chosen caregivers are part of the team. They often know what medicines are actually taken, which symptoms changed first, and what barriers make a plan impossible.

The FNP should be able to answer: Who is responsible for the next clinical decision? Who reviews the pending result? Who changes or refills the medicine? Who confirms the referral occurred? Who will contact the patient? If the answer is “someone else,” but no person or process is named, the task still belongs to the care team and is not safely closed.

Part 2 — Roles, Scope, and Respectful Consultation

Team members bring different expertise. Nursing assessment may identify deterioration, education needs, and functional changes. Pharmacists can clarify medication reconciliation, interactions, access, and monitoring. Social work/care management can address housing, benefits, transport, safety, and navigation. Behavioral-health clinicians assess and treat mental-health/substance-use needs. Rehabilitation professionals evaluate mobility, function, and equipment. Specialists offer focused expertise, procedures, and co-management.

Consultation does not transfer all responsibility. The referring FNP should send a clear question and relevant clinical information, then track completion and recommendations. Scope, delegation, supervision, and collaborative-practice requirements vary by role, state, employer, and setting. When uncertain, verify policy rather than making assumptions about who may perform a task or make a decision.

Part 3 — Shared Care Plan

A useful care plan states the patient’s priorities, active diagnoses, current risks, medicines and allergies, goals, responsible clinician(s), pending tests, upcoming appointments, action thresholds, and return precautions. It should be understandable to the patient and usable by the team. Avoid a list of disconnected recommendations that compete for time, money, and attention.

Prioritize acute safety, then the highest-impact controllable problems. For a patient with heart failure, diabetes, CKD, depression, and food insecurity, a plan may require medication reconciliation, symptom monitoring, renal/electrolyte ownership, nutrition access, behavioral-health follow-up, and explicit escalation instructions. The team should agree on who does what and when—not simply refer the patient to five separate offices.

Part 4 — Structured Communication and Handoffs

Structured tools such as SBAR can make urgent communication more reliable: situation, background, assessment, recommendation. A handoff should include current severity, timeline, baseline, relevant history, medicines/allergies, recent changes, objective findings, completed and pending tests, treatments/response, uncertainty, anticipated problems, and the specific next action. Read-back or questions help confirm shared understanding.

Do not use structure to conceal uncertainty. “Possible sepsis; source unclear; blood culture pending; patient’s BP is falling despite initial measures” communicates more safely than “patient stable for transfer.” The receiving clinician needs to know what has not been excluded and what must happen next.

Part 5 — Medication Coordination

Medication harm often occurs when clinicians independently add, stop, or refill therapies without a shared list or monitoring plan. High-risk situations include hospitalization, emergency visits, specialist changes, renal decline, pregnancy, anticoagulation, insulin, opioids/sedatives, diuretics, and multiple prescribers. The active EHR list may be incomplete or inaccurate; verify what the patient actually uses, including OTC products and supplements.

After a medication change, define indication, dose, expected benefit, important adverse effects, laboratory/clinical monitoring, refill ownership, and follow-up. A pharmacist consultation can be especially valuable when polypharmacy, interactions, affordability, or formulation/device use is involved. Do not assume a pharmacy fill means the patient understands or is taking the medication as intended.

Part 6 — Referrals and Transitions: The Loop Must Close

A referral is a care partnership, not an administrative endpoint. Include the clinical question, urgency, relevant history, data, differential, and what has already been attempted. Confirm receipt, appointment scheduling, completion, consultant recommendation, patient communication, and next-step ownership. If a referral is blocked by access, insurance, transport, records, language, or worsening symptoms, reassess the pathway and the patient’s urgency.

At hospital-to-home or facility-to-community transitions, reconcile diagnoses, uncertainty, pending studies, medicines, function, equipment, services, and follow-up. A discharge summary can be delayed or conflicting. The FNP must compare it with patient/caregiver report, available records, and current assessment rather than copying it forward.

Part 7 — Conflict, Disagreement, and Escalation

Healthy teams may disagree. State the clinical concern, objective facts, patient goal, and requested action without blaming a colleague. Escalate through the appropriate chain when a patient-safety concern is unresolved. Document factual communication and resulting plan. Do not allow hierarchy, discomfort, or assumptions that another clinician “must have seen it” to delay urgent action.

Immediate escalation is needed when there is clinical deterioration, an unreviewed critical result, incompatible medication orders with risk of harm, unclear responsibility for a time-sensitive task, or a patient whose access barrier makes a recommended urgent pathway unsafe. Team communication supports—not replaces—emergency disposition when needed.

Part 8 — Clinical Case: The Conflicting Medication Lists

A patient returns after hospitalization with two discharge lists, a specialist-added diuretic, and a primary-care refill for a drug the hospital stopped. The patient reports dizziness and has CKD.

FNP reasoning: this is not a clerical cleanup. Verify actual use, indication, recent physiology, renal function/electrolytes when indicated, orthostatic symptoms, and each prescriber’s intent. Coordinate promptly with pharmacy and relevant clinicians, communicate one clear plan to the patient, and assign monitoring ownership.

Part 9 — Clinical Case: Referral With No Appointment

A patient with progressive dysphagia has an urgent referral, but the specialty office has no record of it and the patient has lost more weight.

FNP reasoning: the loop is open. Reassess symptoms, hydration/nutrition and red flags; resend/clarify the referral and select an alternative pathway if necessary. If the patient’s trajectory makes waiting unsafe, use urgent or emergency evaluation rather than continuing administrative follow-up alone.

Part 10 — Clinical Case: Speaking Up for Deterioration

A nurse reports that a patient who was comfortable earlier is now confused, tachycardic, and has low urine output. The chart has multiple chronic diagnoses.

FNP reasoning: treat the change from baseline as clinically meaningful. Obtain focused data, reassess the patient, communicate urgency clearly, and escalate according to the patient’s stability. Avoid attributing deterioration to “baseline complexity” without evaluation.

FNP Team-Based Care Framework

  1. Center the patient: goals, preferences, access, caregivers, and functional reality.
  2. Clarify roles: identify the responsible clinician and task owner for each problem.
  3. Communicate deliberately: use structured handoffs and state uncertainty, urgency, and next action.
  4. Reconcile transitions: diagnoses, results, medicines, function, services, and follow-up.
  5. Close loops: referrals and results are not complete until received, acted on, communicated, and owned.
  6. Use expertise: involve pharmacy, nursing, rehabilitation, social work, behavioral health, and specialists early when their skills change safety or outcomes.
  7. Escalate unresolved risk: role confusion, access failure, incompatible orders, deterioration, or critical results require action now.

High-Yield Summary

Interprofessional care: means shared goals, role clarity, communication, and coordinated action—not merely multiple clinicians.
FNP responsibility: clarify ownership; referral or consultation does not erase follow-up responsibility.
Handoff: include severity, history, data, pending issues, uncertainty, contingency plan, and explicit next action.
Medication safety: reconcile actual use and assign monitoring/refill ownership after every meaningful transition.
Referral loop: ordered → received → scheduled → completed → interpreted → communicated → next action owned.
Escalation: speak up for deterioration, time-sensitive risk, or a plan that cannot be safely completed.
FNP standard: make the plan coherent for the patient and accountable for every team member.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Scope, delegation, supervision, documentation, referral, handoff, privacy, emergency response, and team roles must follow current institutional policy, local law, and the individual patient’s presentation.
